title: Visiting the sick
hookLine: whoever visits the sick is in the harvest of the garden until he returns

lines: I WAS SICK, AND YOU DID NOT VISIT ME.
YOU WOULD HAVE FOUND ME WITH HIM.
cards: On the Day of Rising, in a hadith in Sahih Muslim, Allah speaks to a person, and the words are strange. I was sick, He says, and you did not visit Me. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells it.

The person is baffled. My Lord, how could I visit You, when You are the Lord of the worlds? The answer comes back, in paraphrase: did you not know that My servant so-and-so was sick, and you did not visit him?
Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him.

teach.b: The word is 'iyadah, visiting the sick. The hadith in Muslim keeps going, and it widens.
I asked you for food, and you did not feed Me. I asked you for water, and you did not give Me to drink. Each time the same bafflement, and each time the same answer: My servant asked you.
Had you done it, you would have found it with Me. A different hadith in Muslim gives the visit its picture.
Whoever visits a sick person, the Prophet said, remains in the khurfah of the garden until he returns. Someone asked what the khurfah was. The answer: its harvest, its fruit being gathered.
So the walk to the hospital, the time in the plastic chair, the walk back to the car, all of it, in this picture, is time spent picking fruit in Paradise.
Al-Bukhari keeps a short command that puts it next to other basic duties, in paraphrase: feed the hungry, visit the sick, and set the captive free. Notice what the visit doesn't require.
No cure. No perfect words. You're not asked to fix anything.
You're asked to show up, sit near, and go home. Bring nothing but yourself, if that's all you have. The harvest starts at the door.

how: Muslims visit the sick at home and in hospital as a sunnah, often bringing food and making a short supplication for the person's healing, citing the hadith that the visitor is in the harvest of the garden until they return.

o: praying for the sick from home rather than going to them
visiting the sick, a visit that keeps you in the garden's harvest
the yearly feast at the end of Ramadan, spent with family

games.q: visiting the sick — tap the pairs.
p: and you did not visit Me

s: in the hadith, the visitor has to bring a cure
the visit itself is the deed; nothing in it asks you to fix anything.
in Muslim, the visitor remains in the garden's harvest until he returns
the khurfah, the fruit being gathered.
in the hadith qudsi, Allah asks only about prayers missed
He asks about the sick not visited, the hungry not fed, the thirsty not given drink.

games.q: on the Day of Rising you hear: I was sick, and you did not visit Me. what do you answer?
o: You were never sick, my Lord.
how could I visit You, Lord of the worlds?
games.why: the person is baffled, and is told: My servant was sick; had you visited him, you would have found Me with him.

practice: Who do you know who is sick right now, in the hospital, recovering at home, or living with an illness people have stopped asking about?
Let one face come, think how you could reach them, a visit, a call, a message, and find a simple first sentence: how are you, really? If you pray, ask for their healing in your own words.

wordCard.voice: 'Iyadah. Visiting the sick: a visit that, in the hadith, keeps you in the garden's harvest until you come home. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the garden's harvest. Every step to the bedside, in that picture, is fruit being gathered. Until next time.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2569 (hadith qudsi: I was sick and you did not visit Me)
Sahih Muslim 2568 (the visitor is in the khurfah of the garden until he returns)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5649 (feed the hungry, visit the sick, set the captive free)
